title: Sums of Random Variables
intro: The distribution of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their distributions. Some families are closed under it; for the rest, generating functions and the central limit theorem take over.

blocks.tex: P(X + Y = s) = \sum_x p_X(x)\,p_Y(s - x), \qquad f_{X+Y}(s) = \int f_X(x)\,f_Y(s - x)\,dx
blocks.caption: For independent X and Y.

blocks.text: To make a total of $s$, the first variable takes some value $x$ and the second must supply the rest; sum over the ways. Convolving two uniform densities on $[0, 1]$ gives a triangle on $[0, 2]$; three give a piecewise quadratic; twelve already look very normal (the Irwin–Hall distributions). Repeated convolution is how the central limit theorem shows up in practice.

items: Binomial($n, p$) + Binomial($m, p$) = Binomial($n + m, p$).
Gamma($a, \lambda$) + Gamma($b, \lambda$) = Gamma($a + b, \lambda$); in particular sums of exponentials and of chi-squares.
Cauchy: the mean of $n$ standard Cauchys is again standard Cauchy, so averaging does not help at all.

blocks.text: Each of these is easiest to prove with generating functions, which turn convolution into multiplication (Generating Functions (#/probability/toolkit/generating-functions)). Families closed under addition with a rescaling are the stable distributions; the normal is the only one with finite variance.
Means and variances need no convolution
Even when the distribution of a sum is hard, its mean is the sum of the means, and its variance is the sum of the variances for independent terms. Often that is enough.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from math import factorial, comb, floor
# The density of a sum is the convolution of the densities. Irwin-Hall: sum of n uniforms
def irwin_hall_cdf(x, n):
    return sum((-1) ** k * comb(n, k) * (x - k) ** n for k in range(floor(x) + 1)) / factorial(n)
rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
for n in (2, 3, 12):
    s = rng.random((10 ** 6, n)).sum(1)
    print(f"sum of {n:2d} uniforms: P(S <= {n/2 - 0.5}) simulated {np.mean(s <= n/2 - 0.5):.4f}, exact {irwin_hall_cdf(n/2 - 0.5, n):.4f}")
# Discrete convolution: the distribution of three dice by convolving PMFs
die = np.ones(6) / 6
three = np.convolve(np.convolve(die, die), die)       # supports 3..18
print("P(three dice sum to 10) =", round(three[10 - 3], 5), "= 27/216 =", round(27 / 216, 5))
# Sums of independent Poissons are Poisson
a, b = rng.poisson(2, 10 ** 6), rng.poisson(5, 10 ** 6)
print(f"Poisson(2) + Poisson(5): mean {np.mean(a + b):.3f}, variance {np.var(a + b):.3f} (both 7)")

blocks.text: Output of the run: sums of 2, 3 and 12 uniforms match the exact Irwin–Hall CDF (0.125, 0.167 and 0.311 at the points tested). Convolving three dice PMFs gives $P(\text{sum} = 10) = 27/216 = 0.125$. Poisson(2) + Poisson(5) has mean 7.002 and variance 6.996.

blocks.title: Two exponentials
solution: $f(s) = \int_0^s\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\lambda e^{-\lambda(s - x)}\,dx = \lambda^2 s\,e^{-\lambda s}$ for $s\ge0$.

blocks.title: The triangle
blocks.text: $U_1, U_2$ are independent uniforms on $[0, 1]$. Find $P(U_1 + U_2\le1.5)$.
solution: The sum has the triangular density on $[0, 2]$. The region above 1.5 is a small triangle with legs 0.5, area $0.5^2/2 = 0.125$.

blocks.title: Combining arrivals
blocks.text: Two independent streams of requests are Poisson with means 3 and 5 per second. What is the probability of more than 10 requests in a second?
